newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Growing trade gap dims Vietnam's economic glory.
newsitem.headline: Growing trade gap dims Vietnam's economic glory.

text.p: Vietnam said on Monday that its trade deficit leapt to a record $4.0 billion in 1996 as the burgeoning economy sucked in imports faster than it could produce goods for sale abroad.

The government's General Statistics Office estimated the volume of exports for the whole year at $7.1 billion and imports at $11.1 billion, creating a trade gap nearly 82 percent higher than 1995's $2.2 billion.

Analysts said the ballooning trade deficit took the gloss off another year of stellar economic growth and laid bare the shortcomings of the communist government's 10-year-old drive for reform along market lines.

"Our road to development has been paved with glory, but our country still has to overcome many difficulties, trials and challenges," Minister of Planning and Investment Tran Xuan Gia wrote in the weekly Vietnam Investment Review at the weekend.

Gia said gross domestic product (GDP) had grown by 9.5 percent in 1996 -- one of the fastest rates in the world -- while industrial production had increased by 14 percent and inflation had been brought under control to end the year at just 4.5 percent.
However, he said the government was faced with an array of other problems in addition to the trade deficit, which Monday's figures showed was equivalent to about 18 percent of annual GDP.
"If this is not solved, it will lead to the collapse of our trade and payment balance in coming years," Gia said.

Until recently, the government had argued that it was normal for economies in transition to record trade deficits as they import capital goods for the development of industry, which would in the long run generate goods for export.

However, many such imports go to low-productivity, loss-making state enterprises and consumer goods now account for a growing share of the country's imports because years of pent-up demand has been unleashed by an explosion in disposable income.
The statistics office's data probably even under-record the trade gap because smuggled goods, which economists estimate could add another $1.0 billion to the import bill, are not included.
The emergence of a serious deficit has brought calls for a drive to promote local products over imports and stirred debate within the government over the merits of embracing free trade.
Hanoi says it is determined to join the ASEAN Free Trade Area in its plan to reduce tariffs to between zero and five percent within 10 years, but often cites the need to protect local industry.

One of the government's answers to the problem has been to restrict borrowing for imports -- a solution which the United Nations criticised in a report last month as likely to have a less lasting impact than fundamental reform of the trade regime.

"The current set of incentives, regulations and systems for resource allocation appear to be impeding the development of Vietnam's employment-generating and export capacity, and risk promoting excessive imports for the development of uncompetitive industries and a high cost economy," the U.N. report said.
"The short-term risks of rapid trade liberalisation are relatively modest compared to the long-term risks of slow or delayed trade liberalisation," it said.
